summary: First English narrative for the August 1939 Soviet choice between the German offer and the stalled Triple Alliance talks.

narrative.hook: Two delegations want your signature. One arrived by slow boat, cannot sign anything binding, and is stuck behind a veto held by a country that is not in the room. The other is offering a finished document and asking to fly in this week.
narrative.short_setup: It is August 19-21, 1939, in Moscow. British and French military delegations have been negotiating a Triple Alliance since the 11th, having travelled by merchant ship; the British head of mission, Admiral Drax, carries no written authority to conclude a binding convention. On August 14 Voroshilov asked them the question the whole thing turns on: will Poland and Romania let the Red Army cross their territory to reach German forces? Neither delegation can answer for Warsaw, and Poland keeps refusing, on the reasoning that Soviet troops admitted once would not leave. Meanwhile Berlin has been pressing a bilateral non-aggression pact carrying a secret protocol that assigns Finland, Estonia, Latvia, eastern Poland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere; a 200-million-Reichsmark credit agreement was signed on the 19th; Ribbentrop wants to come immediately. And in the east, Soviet and Japanese forces have been fighting an undeclared war at Khalkhin Gol since May, with Zhukov's decisive offensive opening on August 20.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The German offer had the one property the other track lacked: it could actually be concluded. It came with a defined territorial buffer, a signed trade agreement already in hand as earnest, and a counterparty able to commit. It removed the immediate prospect of facing Germany in the west while already fighting Japan in the east — a two-front problem that was not hypothetical that August, it was happening. It bought time, free of a German threat, to keep rebuilding an army that the purges had gutted. And it kept the USSR out of a war over Poland that Britain and France, not the Soviet Union, were treaty-bound to fight.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: A genuine three-power alliance was, in principle, a stronger instrument than a bilateral deal with the power it was meant to contain — and it was the only option that confronted Germany with a real second front rather than removing one. It kept the USSR inside the anti-fascist camp its own diplomacy had occupied since the mid-1930s, and it kept Soviet hands off the partition of Poland and the fate of the Baltic states. The transit impasse was real, but impasses in negotiation are not always permanent, and the pressure of an imminent German move on Poland was pressure on Warsaw and London too, not only on Moscow.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Stalin, with Politburo agreement, signalled to the German ambassador around August 19-21 that Moscow would proceed. The last session of the military talks with Britain and France was held on August 21; they were then suspended indefinitely. Ribbentrop flew in and the pact was signed on the night of August 23-24, dated August 23. The stated Soviet basis was the one Voroshilov had held to since mid-August: without an answer on Polish and Romanian transit, a military convention was impossible, and that answer never came. It was not only the Soviet reading. The American ambassador in Moscow reported to Washington on the very day the pact was signed that Poland's continued refusal had made an Anglo-Franco-Soviet agreement impossible, and that even a late Polish reversal would probably come too late.
narrative.outcome_story: Germany invaded Poland on September 1, without having to weigh Soviet opposition. The USSR entered eastern Poland on September 17 under the secret protocol. Japan's government was reportedly shocked by the pact — its own ally had just signed with its active battlefield opponent — and the fallout contributed to Tokyo seeking the armistice that ended Khalkhin Gol in mid-September. Over the next 22 months the Soviet Union annexed the Baltic states and Bessarabia and fought the Winter War against Finland. On June 22, 1941, Germany broke the pact and invaded. Soviet forces were caught largely unready despite repeated intelligence warnings in the preceding months, and the opening losses were catastrophic. The secret protocol was denied by Moscow until 1989, when the USSR formally acknowledged it.
narrative.hindsight_analysis: Two things are easy to run together here and should not be. The first is whether the reading of the situation was defensible. On the evidence of August 1939 it largely was: the talks that could have produced a second front were blocked on a question neither party at the table controlled, the Western delegations lacked the standing to unblock it, an outside observer reached the same conclusion independently, and there was a shooting war in the east making the two-front risk concrete rather than theoretical. That is a real argument, and it does not depend on knowing what came later. What keeps it from being strong is that the whole structure rested on a German promise with nothing behind it — no verification, no enforcement, nothing but Hitler's word and a shared interest that would expire the moment Germany finished in the west. Buying time from an adversary is only worth what you do with the time. The second thing is the outcome, and it splits. In its own terms the pact delivered: 22 months without a German war, and the buffer it specified. But the time was not converted into readiness. When the invasion came in June 1941, the warnings had been arriving for months and were discounted — a failure of threat assessment centred on Stalin personally, and not something the 1939 decision made inevitable. So the pact bought time and did not buy preparedness, and those are separate failures belonging to separate decisions. There is also a counterfactual that should not be quietly assumed. We do not know that a concluded Triple Alliance would have deterred Hitler; it might equally have brought the USSR into war in September 1939 on someone else's timetable. That question is genuinely open, and the case does not close it. What is not in doubt is the cost side: the pact freed Germany to attack Poland without a second front, and the Soviet Union took part in the partition that followed. A decision can be strategically defensible and still be answerable for what it enabled. Both halves of that sentence are load-bearing.
narrative.decision_principle: An agreement you can actually conclude has real advantages over one you cannot — but only up to the value of the promise behind it. Before trading a stalled option for a closable one, ask what happens on the day the other party's interest in keeping the deal runs out.
narrative.longform_story:
By the third week of August 1939, the Soviet government was running two negotiations at once, and only one of them could be finished.

The first had been under way since the 11th. British and French military delegations were in Moscow to negotiate a Triple Alliance — the three-power military convention that, on paper, would confront Germany with the prospect of war on two fronts if it moved against Poland. The delegations had travelled to the USSR by merchant ship, the City of Exeter, rather than by air or fast warship. Admiral Reginald Drax, heading the British mission, carried no written authority to conclude a binding military convention.

On August 14, Voroshilov put the question that decided everything. If war came, would Poland and Romania permit Soviet troops to cross their territory to engage German forces? Without transit rights, the Red Army could not reach the Germans at all, and a convention promising Soviet action would promise nothing.

Neither delegation could answer. They were not authorised to answer for Warsaw, and Warsaw would not give the answer. Poland's government, under Foreign Minister Jozef Beck, refused to consent — on reasoning that was not unfounded and that Polish history made difficult to dismiss: Soviet forces admitted to Polish territory might not leave it.

Voroshilov told the delegations plainly that without a positive answer, all efforts toward a military convention were doomed to fail. He held that position through the last committee session on August 21, after which the talks were suspended.

The second negotiation had been developing in parallel, with Berlin pressing harder as August went on. Germany offered a bilateral non-aggression treaty, and attached to it a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe: Finland, Estonia, Latvia, eastern Poland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere. On August 19 the two governments signed a commercial credit agreement giving the USSR a 200-million-Reichsmark line of credit for German industrial goods — presented by German officials as the first step in reshaping the political relationship, which is exactly what it was. Ribbentrop asked to fly to Moscow immediately.

There was a third thing happening, less remembered, and it mattered enormously. Since May, Soviet and Japanese forces had been fighting a large undeclared war at Khalkhin Gol on the Mongolian-Manchurian frontier — more than a hundred thousand troops between them. Zhukov's decisive offensive opened on August 20, in the middle of all this. The two-front scenario that Soviet planners feared in the abstract was, that month, half-real: one of the fronts already had shooting on it.

So the choice was not between an alliance and a pact. It was between a negotiation blocked on a veto held by a party not at the table, conducted by men who could not sign, with no timetable — and a finished document, with a defined buffer and a counterparty who could commit, available this week.

Stalin took the pact. Agreement was signalled around August 19-21; the military talks held their last session on the 21st; Ribbentrop flew in and the treaty was signed on the night of August 23-24, dated August 23.

The Soviet justification was the one Voroshilov had been giving for ten days. It is worth noting that it was not only the Soviet reading of events. Laurence Steinhardt, the American ambassador in Moscow, reported to Washington on August 23 itself that Poland's continued refusal had made an Anglo-Franco-Soviet agreement impossible, and that even a late Polish reversal would likely arrive too late to prevent a German-Soviet agreement. An outside observer with no stake in excusing Moscow reached the same structural conclusion, on the same day.

Germany invaded Poland on September 1. The Soviet Union entered eastern Poland on September 17, under the protocol. In Tokyo, the pact landed as a shock — Japan's nominal partner under the Anti-Comintern Pact had just signed with the power Japanese soldiers were fighting in Mongolia — and the political fallout contributed to Japan seeking an armistice, concluded in mid-September. Over the following 22 months, the USSR annexed the Baltic states and Bessarabia and fought the Winter War against Finland, broadly along the protocol's lines.

On June 22, 1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union.

How to score this requires keeping several things apart that the drama pulls together.

The strategic reading was defensible on August 1939 evidence. The alliance track was blocked on a question nobody in the room could resolve. The delegations lacked standing. A neutral observer independently judged it dead. A real war was already running in the east. None of that requires hindsight, and none of it is special pleading.

What keeps the decision from rating higher is the nature of what it rested on. The pact had no verification mechanism and no enforcement. It was a promise from Hitler, backed by a convergence of interest that would last exactly as long as Germany was busy elsewhere. Everyone involved understood this was temporary. The strategic case for the pact was therefore not really 'we are now safe' but 'we have bought time' — and time is only worth what is done with it.

Which is where the outcome divides. In the pact's own terms it worked: 22 months of no German war, and the territorial buffer as specified. But the time was not converted. When Barbarossa came, warnings had been arriving for months through multiple channels and were discounted at the top. That was a failure of threat assessment centred on Stalin personally in 1941, not a consequence the 1939 decision made inevitable. The pact bought time; the failure to use it belongs to a different decision, made by the same man, two years later.

One more thing should not be smuggled in. It is tempting to score the pact against a counterfactual in which the Triple Alliance came together and deterred Hitler. We do not know that. It is equally possible that a concluded alliance would have brought the USSR into the war in September 1939 on the Western powers' schedule rather than its own. Historians have not settled this, and neither will a case study. What can be said is narrower: the transit impasse was real, and no account of Western good faith or bad faith makes it disappear.

The historiography is genuinely divided on two further points, and both are worth naming rather than picking. Some historians, Geoffrey Roberts among them, read the pact as a defensive, buffer-seeking response to failed Western talks, and hold that Hitler's timetable for Poland was set regardless of Moscow's alignment. Others treat the pact as the decisive factor that removed Germany's two-front risk and made the September 1 date possible. The documentary record supports that Hitler wanted the pact specifically to neutralise the Soviet factor before attacking; how much the timing depended on getting it is not resolved. Similarly, the slow boat, the junior delegations and the missing full powers support a reading of Anglo-French half-heartedness — but others argue London and Paris were genuinely constrained, reluctant to alarm Poland and disbelieving that Stalin would deal with Hitler at all, and that the failure was mutual mistrust rather than one side's bad faith.

What is not contested is the cost side of the ledger. The pact freed Germany to attack Poland without facing a second front, and the Soviet Union participated in the partition that followed and in the absorption of the Baltic states. Moscow denied the secret protocol existed until 1989.

A decision can be strategically defensible on the information available and still be answerable for what it enabled. Those are two different judgments, and this case is one of the clearest demonstrations of why a serious account has to make both.
